Where it began

Martin Crowe was born on 22 September 1962 in Henderson, on the edge of Auckland, into a family steeped in sport. His father, Dave, was a first-class cricketer with Canterbury and later Wellington, his older brother Jeff went on to play Tests for New Zealand, and his great-grandfather Francis Jervis was an All Black. The actor Russell Crowe is a first cousin.

In 1968 he followed his father and brother to the Cornwall club, and he stayed loyal to it all his life. At Auckland Grammar he captained the cricket team, played on the wing at rugby and was deputy head boy. He made his debut for Auckland at 17, top-scoring with 51, and in 1981 spent six months on the Lord's ground staff.

The player

His Test debut came in Wellington in February 1982, when he was 19. Wisden made him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1985, and in 1991, as captain, he made 299 against Sri Lanka at the Basin Reserve, the highest Test score by a New Zealander at the time. He and Andrew Jones added 467 together, then a record for any wicket in Tests, as New Zealand, 323 behind on first innings, batted on to 671 for 4.

He played 77 Tests from 1982 to 1995 and made 5,444 runs at 45.37, with 17 hundreds and 18 fifties. When he finished, both his Test runs and his hundreds were New Zealand records, and he had made a century against every Test side bar South Africa.

What made him special

He was a big man who batted upright and orthodox, with quick, graceful feet. As a captain he liked to try things. At the 1992 World Cup, played at home and in Australia, he opened the bowling with the off-spinner Dipak Patel, took his side to the semi-finals and was named player of the tournament after making 456 runs.

His bowling was more of a sideline. His lively in-swingers did well enough in England, but 14 Test wickets at 48.29 suggest he was right to put his energy into batting.

Away from the middle

After his playing days he helped develop Cricket Max, a home-grown variant of the game, and became a commentator and writer. He was one of the people behind the idea of a World Test Championship, and he mentored the younger New Zealand batters Kane Williamson, Ross Taylor and Martin Guptill. In 2014 he named Williamson, Joe Root, Steve Smith and Virat Kohli as the coming Fab Four of Test batting, which turned out to be a very good call.

He was made an MBE in 1992, was inducted into the ICC's Hall of Fame in 2015, and was named in New Zealand Cricket's Hall of Fame First XI in 2024. He died in Auckland in March 2016.

And finally

At 49 he decided he fancied another go, and turned out for Cornwall's reserve grade, captaining the side and batting at three. Some people take up golf. Martin Crowe went back to the club where he had started.
